subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 12 periods = 540 minutes
Total: 12 periods · 9h 0min

periods.activity_title: Can Every Number Be a Sum of Consecutive Numbers?

textbook_items_in_class.description: Explore whether every natural number, every even number, and 0 (using negatives) can be written as a sum of consecutive numbers; discuss with class.
Take four consecutive numbers; place '+' and '−' signs between them in all eight ways; list all possibilities.
Evaluate each of the eight expressions formed from 3, 4, 5, 6; record results; repeat for another set of four consecutive numbers; share findings.
Take any four consecutive numbers; place '+'/'-' signs in all eight ways; observe parities; repeat for another set.

time_bands.activity: Math Talk Q1, section 5.1 p.112 ("Explore whether every natural number, every even number, and 0....") — students try small cases (1, 2, 3, …, 10) to decide which can and cannot be expressed as sums of consecutive numbers, recording findings in pairs.

Math Talk Q2, section 5.1 p.112 ("Take four consecutive numbers; place '+' and '−' signs....") — groups list all eight sign combinations for a chosen set of four consecutive numbers, then share and compare lists to confirm all eight are accounted for.

Math Talk Q3, section 5.1 p.113 ("Evaluate each of the eight expressions formed from 3, 4, 5, 6....") — students evaluate all eight expressions for {3,4,5,6} and a second self-chosen set, recording each result; the class pools results and notices all outcomes are even.

Math Talk Q4, section 5.1 p.113 ("Take any four consecutive numbers; place '+'/'-' signs in all eight ways....") — pairs check parity for a third set of four consecutive numbers, then a brief whole-class share surfaces the conjecture: all eight expressions share parity.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often assume the parity observation breaks for larger numbers; encourage a second pair to test a set starting above 20 to widen the evidence base. Watch for the common error of listing fewer than eight sign combinations — a quick class count before evaluation saves time. The conjecture that all eight expressions are even (rather than merely sharing parity with one another) is a productive over-generalisation worth noting without resolving yet.
materials: Squared or plain paper for recording

periods.activity_title: Why Parity Never Changes: Three Algebraic Proofs

textbook_items_in_class.description: Is there a way to explain why all eight expressions from four numbers share parity? Hint: parity rules for sum/difference of two numbers.
Replace any negative sign in a + b − c − d with positive; find the difference between the two numbers; conclude.

Algebraic proof that switching any '+' or '−' sign between four numbers changes the value by 2 times the affected number (an even amount), so all eight expressions formed from four numbers share the same parity.
Parity-rules proof that a ± b always has the same parity, extending to show all expressions a ± b ± c ± d share parity.
Is the phenomenon of all expressions having the same parity limited to four numbers? Investigate.

time_bands.activity: Math Talk Q5, section 5.1 p.114 ("Is there a way to explain why all eight expressions from four numbers share parity?...") — students attempt a written explanation in their own words before any formal proof is introduced, drawing on the parity-rules hint.

Explanation 1, section 5.1 p.114 ("Algebraic proof that switching any '+' or '−' sign changes the value by 2 times....") — teacher walks through the sign-switching argument; Math Talk Q6, section 5.1 p.114 ("Replace any negative sign … find the difference....") is used as an immediate check, with students verifying the claim for a numeric example.

Explanation 2, section 5.1 p.114 ("Parity-rules proof that a ± b always has the same parity....") — teacher presents the second proof; students then reconstruct the chain a ± b ± c ± d in their notebooks, annotating each step with the parity rule applied.

Math Talk Q7, section 5.1 p.115 ("Is the phenomenon of all expressions having the same parity limited to four numbers?...") — pairs investigate with five and six numbers, sharing initial findings; the unit closes with the class articulating an extended conjecture in plain language.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established through exploration that all eight expressions share parity, students now need to see why sign-switching changes the value by exactly 2 times the affected number — a step many initially find surprising. A common error is conflating 'all results are even' with 'all results are equal'; Explanation 1 is the clearest place to address this distinction. For students who finish early, point them to the token-model approach described in the chapter's third explanation (Explanation 3, section 5.1 p.114) as a self-study pointer.

periods.activity_title: Breaking Even and Pairs to Make Fours

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Breaking Even — arithmetic expressions, section 5.1 p.115
textbook_items_in_class.description: Without computing, determine which of the eight arithmetic expressions (43+37; 672−348; 4×347×3; 708−477; 809+214; 119×303; 543−479; 513³) are even.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Breaking Even — algebraic expressions, section 5.1 p.115
textbook_items_in_class.description: Identify which algebraic expressions (2a+2b; 3g+5h; 4m+2n; 2u−4v; 13k−5k; 6m−3n; x²+2; b²+1; 4k×3j) always give an even number for any integer values; give examples and non-examples for each.
Two justifications that 4m + 2q is always even: (i) both 4m and 2q are individually even; (ii) factoring gives 2(2m + q), showing 2 is a factor. Contrasted with x² + 2, which is not always even.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Pairs to Make Fours Q1, section 5.1 p.116
textbook_items_in_class.description: Take a pair of even numbers, add them, check if divisible by 4; try different pairs; find when the sum is a multiple of 4 and when not; identify a general rule.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Pairs to Make Fours table, section 5.1 p.117
textbook_items_in_class.description: Algebraic and visualisation proof for three cases: 4p + 4q = 4(p+q) always multiple of 4; (4p+2) + (4q+2) = 4(p+q+1) always multiple of 4; 4p + (4q+2) = 4(p+q)+2 never a multiple of 4.

homework.book_ref: Breaking Even — write algebraic expressions, section 5.1 p.116
homework.description: Write a few algebraic expressions that always give an even number.

time_bands.activity: Breaking Even — arithmetic expressions, section 5.1 p.115 ("Without computing, determine which of the eight arithmetic expressions are even....") — individuals work silently, using only parity rules; pairs then compare answers and resolve disagreements.

Breaking Even — algebraic expressions, section 5.1 p.115 ("Identify which algebraic expressions always give an even number....") — groups classify each expression, supplying a numeric example and a non-example for borderline cases, then compare with Example, section 5.1 p.116 ("Two justifications that 4m + 2q is always even....") to check reasoning.

Pairs to Make Fours Q1, section 5.1 p.116 ("Take a pair of even numbers, add them, check if divisible by 4....") — students collect a table of even-number pairs and their sums, sorting entries by divisibility by 4 and noticing the two classes of even numbers.

Pairs to Make Fours table, section 5.1 p.117 ("Algebraic and visualisation proof for three cases....") — teacher presents the algebraic and visual arguments for all three cases; students annotate the table in their notebooks with the corresponding algebraic identity.

periods.teacher_notes: Building on the parity invariance established earlier, this unit distinguishes two families of even numbers — multiples of 4 and non-multiples of 4 — which many students find surprising since they tend to treat 'even' as a single category. A frequent error in the algebraic expressions task is claiming 3g + 5h is always even without testing odd values; insist on at least one non-example before accepting a claim. Breaking Even — write algebraic expressions, section 5.1 p.116, is set as reinforcement to consolidate the factoring insight.

periods.activity_title: Always, Sometimes, or Never: Five Divisibility Statements

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Always, Sometimes, or Never — examine statements, section 5.1 p.118
textbook_items_in_class.description: We know the sum of two multiples of 2 is a multiple of 2. Determine if statement 1 (if 8 divides two numbers separately it divides their sum) is also true with subtraction.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Always, Sometimes, or Never Q2, section 5.1 p.119
textbook_items_in_class.description: Examine statement 2: if a number is divisible by 8, then 8 also divides any two numbers that add up to it — is this always, sometimes, or never true?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Always, Sometimes, or Never Q3, section 5.1 p.119
textbook_items_in_class.description: Examine statement 3: if a number is divisible by 7, all multiples of that number are divisible by 7 — always, sometimes, or never true?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Always, Sometimes, or Never Q4, section 5.1 p.120
textbook_items_in_class.description: Examine statement 4: if a number is divisible by 12, it is also divisible by all factors of 12 — always, sometimes, or never true?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Always, Sometimes, or Never Q5, section 5.1 p.120
textbook_items_in_class.description: Examine statement 5: if a number is divisible by 7, it is also divisible by any multiple of 7 — always, sometimes, or never true?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Always, Sometimes, or Never — statements 1–5, section 5.1 pp.118–120
textbook_items_in_class.description: Five worked statements about divisibility (by 8, 7, 12, 6) classified as always/sometimes/never true with algebraic proofs, visualisations, and examples; establishes four general divisibility laws.

time_bands.activity: Always, Sometimes, or Never — examine statements, section 5.1 p.118 ("Determine if statement 1 is also true with subtraction....") — students first vote on their initial guess (always/sometimes/never) before any calculation, surfacing intuitive assumptions.

Always, Sometimes, or Never Q2–Q3, section 5.1 pp.119 ("Examine statement 2… statement 3....") — pairs work through each statement by constructing an algebraic argument or a counterexample; brief class discussion after each.

Always, Sometimes, or Never Q4–Q5, section 5.1 pp.120 ("Examine statement 4… statement 5....") — groups tackle both remaining statements; teacher circulates, prompting students who rely only on examples to move toward an algebraic general argument.

Always, Sometimes, or Never — statements 1–5, section 5.1 pp.118–120 ("Five worked statements … establishes four general divisibility laws....") — class reviews the four general laws together; students record each law in their own words alongside the algebraic form.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established the algebraic forms for multiples of 4, students are now ready to reason about divisibility by larger numbers using the same approach. The most persistent error here is accepting a few confirming examples as proof — especially for Statement 3, where students quickly find multiples of 7 and conclude 'always' without a general argument. Press for the algebraic form: if A = 7k, then any multiple of A is 7kn, and 7 divides 7kn.

periods.activity_title: What Remains? Remainder Arithmetic and Figure it Out

textbook_items_in_class.description: Find a number that has a remainder of 3 when divided by 5; write more such numbers.
Which algebraic expression(s) capture all numbers leaving remainder 3 when divided by 5: (i) 3k+5; (ii) 3k−5; (iii) 3k/5; (iv) 5k+3; (v) 5k−2; (vi) 5k−3?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.1 p.122
textbook_items_in_class.description: The sum of four consecutive numbers is 34. What are these numbers?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 5.1 p.122
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find numbers leaving remainder 2 when divided by both 3 and 4. Write an algebraic expression for all such numbers.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 5.1 p.122
textbook_items_in_class.description: Pebble riddle: number leaves remainder 1 when grouped by 3 or 5, is divisible by 7, and is less than 100. Find the number.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 5.1 p.123
textbook_items_in_class.description: 661 leaves remainder 3 and 4779 leaves remainder 5 when divided by 7. Without calculating, find the remainders when (i) 4779 + 661 and (ii) 4779 − 661 are divided by 7; show algebraically and visually.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 5.1 p.123
homework.description: Find the smallest number that leaves remainder 2 when divided by 3, remainder 3 when divided by 4, and remainder 4 when divided by 5. Explain why it is the smallest.

time_bands.activity: What Remains? Q1–Q2, section 5.1 pp.121 ("Find a number with remainder 3 when divided by 5; which expressions capture all such numbers?...") — students list several examples, then evaluate each expression option by testing specific values of k.

Figure it Out Q1, section 5.1 p.122 ("The sum of four consecutive numbers is 34. What are these numbers?...") and Figure it Out Q4, section 5.1 p.122 ("Find numbers leaving remainder 2 when divided by both 3 and 4....") — students set up algebraic expressions using n, n+1, … and remainder forms to solve both problems systematically.

Figure it Out Q5, section 5.1 p.122 ("Pebble riddle: number leaves remainder 1 when grouped by 3 or 5, divisible by 7, less than 100....") — groups use a systematic search guided by the algebraic form 3k+1 ∩ 5j+1, then check divisibility by 7.

Figure it Out Q7, section 5.1 p.123 ("661 leaves remainder 3 and 4779 leaves remainder 5 when divided by 7....") — students write 661 = 7a + 3 and 4779 = 7b + 5, then add and subtract to find remainders; a visual approach using number-line segments is also demonstrated.

periods.teacher_notes: The general divisibility laws proved in the 'Always, Sometimes, or Never' subsection are precisely the tools students need here — particularly the rule about remainders under addition and subtraction. A common error in Q7 is computing 3 + 5 = 8 and giving 8 as the remainder without reducing modulo 7; prompt students to check whether their remainder is less than the divisor. Figure it Out Q8 (p.123) is assigned as reinforcement for the three-simultaneous-remainder strategy.

periods.activity_title: Completing Section 5.1 and Place-Value Roots of Divisibility

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Always, Sometimes, or Never — extra statements, section 5.1 p.121
textbook_items_in_class.description: Determine for statements 6–8: (6) if divisible by both 9 and 4, must be divisible by 36; (7) if divisible by both 6 and 4, must be divisible by 24; (8) odd + even gives a multiple of 6 — always, sometimes, or never true.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 5.1 p.122
textbook_items_in_class.description: For five statements, determine always/sometimes/never true with algebraic justification: (i) sum of two even numbers is a multiple of 3; (ii) not divisible by 18 implies not divisible by 9; (iii) if two numbers not divisible by 6, sum not divisible by 6; (iv) sum of multiple of 6 and multiple of 9 is multiple of 3; (v) sum of multiple of 6 and multiple of 3 is multiple of 9.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Divisibility by 10 — place-value algebra, section 5.2 p.123
textbook_items_in_class.description: Derivation using the general form …1000d + 100c + 10b + a showing all place values except units are multiples of 10, proving the divisibility-by-10 rule; students extend this to 5, 2, 4, 8.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.2 p.123
textbook_items_in_class.description: Explain using algebra why divisibility shortcuts for 5, 2, 4, and 8 work.

time_bands.activity: Always, Sometimes, or Never — extra statements, section 5.1 p.121 ("Determine for statements 6–8 — divisibility by 9 and 4 implying 36, etc....") and Figure it Out Q3, section 5.1 p.122 ("For five statements, determine always/sometimes/never true....") — students work in pairs, using the four general divisibility laws to classify each statement and write a one-line algebraic justification.

Divisibility by 10 — place-value algebra, section 5.2 p.123 ("Derivation using …1000d + 100c + 10b + a showing all place values except units are multiples of 10....") — teacher develops the general expanded form on the board; students write the parallel derivation for divisibility by 10, then predict what happens for 5 and 2 before the teacher confirms.

Figure it Out Q1, section 5.2 p.123 ("Explain using algebra why divisibility shortcuts for 5, 2, 4, and 8 work....") — individuals write the algebraic explanation for each of the four shortcuts, using the last 1, 2, or 3 digits as appropriate; pairs check each other's reasoning.

periods.teacher_notes: Statement 7 in the extra statements (divisibility by 6 and 4 implying 24) is a productive trap — LCM of 6 and 4 is 12, not 24, and students discover this by finding a counterexample. The move into section 5.2 is motivated by asking: 'The place-value form explains shortcuts for 2, 5, 10 easily — what about 9?' This question primes curiosity for the digit-sum derivation that follows. Watch for students who confuse 'divisible by 4 means last two digits divisible by 4' with 'last two digits form a number divisible by 4' — they are the same thing, but the phrasing trips some learners.

periods.activity_title: Why the Digit Sum Rules Work: Proofs for 9 and 3

textbook_items_in_class.description: Can any number made of only digits '0' and '9' (in any order) always be divisible by 9?
Is 10 divisible by 9? What is the remainder? Check other multiples of 10 (10, 20, 30, …) divided by 9; observe the pattern.
Look at remainders when multiples of 100 are divided by 9; what do you notice?
Using the place-value remainder observation, find the remainder when 427 is divided by 9.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Shortcut for Divisibility by 9, section 5.2 pp.124–125
textbook_items_in_class.description: Proof that the remainder when any number is divided by 9 equals the sum of its digits, using the decomposition 10^n = (10^n − 1) + 1 where 10^n − 1 is always a repunit multiple of 9. Worked example with 7309.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk — divisibility by 3, section 5.2 p.126
textbook_items_in_class.description: A number is divisible by 3 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3. Explore remainders when powers of 10 are divided by 3 and explain why the method works.

time_bands.activity: Math Talk Q1–Q3, section 5.2 pp.124 ("Can any number made of only digits '0' and '9' always be divisible by 9?... Is 10 divisible by 9?... Look at remainders when multiples of 100 are divided by 9....") — students build a table of remainders for 10, 100, 1000, … on division by 9, noticing the remainder is always 1.

Math Talk Q4, section 5.2 p.124 ("Using the place-value remainder observation, find the remainder when 427 is divided by 9....") — pairs apply the pattern to 427 by summing digits, then verify with long division; findings are shared briefly.

Shortcut for Divisibility by 9, section 5.2 pp.124–125 ("Proof that the remainder … equals the sum of its digits, using 10^n = (10^n − 1) + 1....") — teacher presents the formal proof; students annotate each step, then independently apply the method to 7309 and a number of their own choosing.

Math Talk — divisibility by 3, section 5.2 p.126 ("Explore remainders when powers of 10 are divided by 3 and explain why the method works....") — students repeat the remainder-table exercise for powers of 10 divided by 3, noticing remainders are all 1, and articulate the parallel argument for the digit-sum rule for 3.

periods.teacher_notes: The key insight — that every power of 10 leaves remainder 1 when divided by 9 — is best discovered by students themselves before the proof is stated; the Math Talk sequence is designed for this. A common error is adding digits and checking divisibility without appreciating that the digit sum equals the remainder (not just that it signals divisibility); emphasise that 427 has digit sum 13, remainder 13 mod 9 = 4, not remainder 0. Students who grasp divisibility by 9 quickly can be invited to look at Math Talk Q6, section 5.2 p.125 for a more careful biconditional analysis.

periods.activity_title: The Alternating Digit Rule: Proving Divisibility by 11

textbook_items_in_class.description: Using the alternating place-value pattern, determine whether 462 is divisible by 11.
What is a general method or shortcut to check divisibility by 11?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Shortcut for Divisibility by 11, section 5.2 pp.127–128
textbook_items_in_class.description: Proof of the alternating digit-sum rule for divisibility by 11 using the pattern that 10^n is alternately 1 more or 1 less than a multiple of 11. Two equivalent methods shown; worked example with 320185.
If the difference between the two digit-sum groups is 11 or a multiple of 11, what does that say about the remainder when the number is divided by 11?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Divisibility by 11 — check six numbers, section 5.2 p.128
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using the shortcut, determine whether (i) 158; (ii) 841; (iii) 481; (iv) 5529; (v) 90904; (vi) 857076 are divisible by 11; find remainder if not.
Is the alternating-signs method (place '−' and '+' alternately before digits from units place, evaluate expression) similar to or different from the two-sum method for divisibility by 11?

time_bands.activity: Math Talk Q1–Q2, section 5.2 pp.127 ("Using the alternating place-value pattern, determine whether 462 is divisible by 11?... What is a general method or shortcut?...") — students build a remainder table for powers of 10 divided by 11, noticing the alternating 1, −1 pattern, then articulate an informal shortcut.

Shortcut for Divisibility by 11, section 5.2 pp.127–128 ("Proof of the alternating digit-sum rule … two equivalent methods; worked example with 320185....") — teacher presents the formal proof; students follow along and verify with 320185, then construct the argument for a four-digit number independently.

Divisibility by 11 — check six numbers, section 5.2 p.128 ("Determine whether 158; 841; 481; 5529; 90904; 857076 are divisible by 11....") — individuals apply the shortcut to all six numbers, recording the alternating digit sums and their differences; pairs check results.

Math Talk Q3–Q4, section 5.2 pp.128–129 ("If the difference is 11 or a multiple of 11 … what does that say about remainder?... Is the alternating-signs method similar to the two-sum method?...") — class discusses both questions, establishing that the two methods are equivalent and that any difference that is a multiple of 11 implies divisibility.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who handled the digit-sum proof for 9 fluently often struggle here because the alternating sign is conceptually new — clarify that 10 ≡ −1 (mod 11) is the key fact driving the alternation. A common error is computing the absolute difference of the two digit groups and declaring divisibility only when the difference is 0, missing cases where the difference is 11 or 22. For self-study, Math Talk Q4, section 5.2 p.129 invites students to confirm algebraically that the alternating-signs method and the two-group method are identical in effect.

periods.activity_title: Digital Roots, Composite Shortcuts, and the Divisibility Table

textbook_items_in_class.description: Examine which of four statements about divisibility by 9 and digit sums are correct: (i) divisible by 9 ⟹ digit sum divisible by 9; (ii) digit sum divisible by 9 ⟹ divisible by 9; (iii) not divisible by 9 ⟹ digit sum not divisible by 9; (iv) digit sum not divisible by 9 ⟹ not divisible by 9.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: More on Divisibility Shortcuts Q1, section 5.2 p.129
textbook_items_in_class.description: How can we find if a number is divisible by 6? Will checking divisibility by 2 and 3 work? Verify with 38, 225, 186, 64.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: More on Divisibility Shortcuts Q2, section 5.2 p.130
textbook_items_in_class.description: How about checking divisibility by 24 — does checking factors 4 and 6 work? Why or why not? Explain using prime factorisation why checking 3 and 8 works instead.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Fill in the table, section 5.2 p.129
textbook_items_in_class.description: Complete the divisibility table for ten numbers (128, 990, 1586, 275, 6686, 639210, 429714, 2856, 3060, 406839) against divisors 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11.
What property does the digital root have? Recall how it connects to divisibility by 9.
Write the digital roots of any 12 consecutive numbers. What do you observe?

homework.description: Find the digital roots of some consecutive multiples of (i) 3; (ii) 4; (iii) 6.

time_bands.activity: Math Talk Q6, section 5.2 p.125 ("Examine which of four statements about divisibility by 9 and digit sums are correct....") — students classify each statement as true or false, giving a brief algebraic or numeric reason; the biconditional structure (both directions hold) is confirmed.

More on Divisibility Shortcuts Q1–Q2, section 5.2 pp.129–130 ("Will checking divisibility by 2 and 3 work for 6?... Does checking 4 and 6 work for 24?...") — students explore using LCM thinking; the prime-factorisation argument for why coprime factors must be checked is developed in pairs.

Fill in the table, section 5.2 p.129 ("Complete the divisibility table for ten numbers against divisors 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11....") — individuals complete the table efficiently, applying all shortcuts learned so far; the teacher spot-checks divisibility by 11 and 9 for a few rows.

Digital Roots Q1, section 5.2 p.130 ("What property does the digital root have?...") and Digital Roots Q3, section 5.2 p.130 ("Write the digital roots of any 12 consecutive numbers. What do you observe?...") — pairs compute digital roots for 12 consecutive numbers, discovering the cycling pattern, then articulate the connection to remainders on division by 9.

periods.teacher_notes: The composite-shortcut discussion (Q2) is the pivot point between procedural rules and the underlying LCM reasoning; students who understand why 3 and 8 work for 24 but 4 and 6 do not are demonstrating genuine number-theoretic insight. A frequent error in the divisibility table is ticking a number as divisible by 6 if it is divisible by 2 or 3 rather than both; prompt with: 'What does divisible by 6 mean in terms of factors?' Digital Roots Q4, section 5.2 p.130, is set as reinforcement to explore how the digital-root cycle shifts for multiples of 3 and 6.

periods.activity_title: Digital Root Puzzles and the First Cryptarithms

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.2 p.131
textbook_items_in_class.description: The digital root of an 8-digit number is 5. What is the digital root of 10 more than that number?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 5.2 p.131
textbook_items_in_class.description: What is the digital root of the number 9a + 36b + 13?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 5.2 p.131
textbook_items_in_class.description: Make conjectures about (i) the parity of a number and its digital root; (ii) the digital root of a number and the remainder when divided by 3 or 9.
Solve addition cryptarithm (i): A1 + 1B = B0.
Solve addition cryptarithm (ii): AB + 37 = 6A.
Solve addition cryptarithm (iii): ON + ON + ON = PO.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q1, Q3, Q4, section 5.2 p.131 ("The digital root of an 8-digit number is 5…; what is the digital root of 9a + 36b + 13?; make conjectures about parity and digital roots....") — students work through all three items individually, then share conjectures with a partner; teacher facilitates a brief class discussion of Q4's two conjectures.

Cryptarithms Q1, section 5.3 p.131 ("Solve addition cryptarithm A1 + 1B = B0....") — the cryptarithm genre is introduced; students analyse what each column tells them about carries and digit constraints, working in pairs.

Cryptarithms Q2–Q3, section 5.3 p.131 ("Solve AB + 37 = 6A.... Solve ON + ON + ON = PO....") — pairs tackle each cryptarithm in turn; groups who finish Q2 move directly to Q3; teacher prompts students to write explicit constraints before guessing.

Cryptarithms Q4, section 5.3 p.131 ("Solve addition cryptarithm QR + QR + QR = PRR....") — this more complex cryptarithm is attempted by individuals; the class shares solution strategies, surfacing different entry points (units column first vs. estimating the product).

periods.teacher_notes: The digital root of 9a + 36b + 13 reduces to the digital root of 13 (which is 4) because 9a and 36b are both multiples of 9; students who see this quickly have deeply understood the digit-sum proof from section 5.2. The cryptarithms introduce a new genre of puzzle — watch for students who substitute random digits rather than deriving constraints column by column; encourage writing 'units column: 1 + B must end in 0' as a first step. Cryptarithm Q4 (QR + QR + QR = PRR) is best approached by noting that 3 × QR produces a three-digit number, so QR ≥ 34.

periods.activity_title: Multiplication Cryptarithms: Reasoning Digit by Digit

textbook_items_in_class.description: Solve multiplication cryptarithm (v): PQ × 8 = RS.
Worked solution showing that only PQ = 12 satisfies the constraint that a 2-digit number times 8 gives a 2-digit number with distinct digits.
Solve multiplication cryptarithm (vi): GH × H = 9K. Choose from the options given.
What can you say about 'Y' in BYE × 6 = RAY? What digits are possible or not possible for Y?
Guided reasoning: B = 1 (product must stay 3-digit), Y must be even and less than 7; students deduce remaining digits.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Solve the following Q1, section 5.3 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: Solve multiplication cryptarithm: UT × 3 = PUT.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Solve the following Q2, section 5.3 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: Solve multiplication cryptarithm: AB × 5 = BC.

homework.book_ref: Solve the following Q3, section 5.3 p.132

time_bands.activity: Cryptarithms Q5, section 5.3 p.131 ("Solve PQ × 8 = RS....") — students attempt to narrow the range for PQ (must be ≤ 12 for the product to stay two-digit) before the worked example is revealed; pairs share their bounding argument.

Cryptarithm PQ × 8 = RS, section 5.3 p.131 ("Worked solution showing only PQ = 12 satisfies constraints....") — teacher walks through the worked solution; Cryptarithms Q6, section 5.3 p.132 ("GH × H = 9K....") is then attempted by pairs using the same bounding strategy.

Cryptarithms Q7, section 5.3 p.132 ("What can you say about Y in BYE × 6 = RAY?...") — students list constraints on Y (must be even; product of Y × 6 must end in Y; Y < 7); after pairs commit to a list, Cryptarithm BYE × 6 = RAY, section 5.3 p.132 ("Guided reasoning: B = 1, Y even and less than 7....") is used to complete the solution.

Solve the following Q1–Q2, section 5.3 p.132 ("UT × 3 = PUT.... AB × 5 = BC....") — individuals work on both; teacher circulates and asks 'What does the units column tell you first?' to redirect students who start with the tens column.

periods.teacher_notes: Multiplication cryptarithms require students to combine digit-constraint reasoning (units digit of product determines a letter) with magnitude reasoning (product must have the right number of digits); keeping both in play simultaneously is the chief difficulty at this stage. A common error in UT × 3 = PUT is not noticing that the three-digit product implies 3 × UT ≥ 100, so UT ≥ 34 — begin by bounding before substituting. Solve the following Q3, section 5.3 p.132 (L2N × 2 = 2NP) is set as reinforcement for the digit-by-digit bounding strategy.

periods.activity_title: Number Play: Four Problems, Every Method
periods.teacher_notes: Pose all four problems at once. Students work individually with full written working for the first stretch, then compare in groups of three — any disagreement is resolved by reconstructing the solution step by step, not by majority vote. One student per group presents one problem; after each presentation the class names the chapter method the solution rested on. Problem 1 needs remainder-class algebra (section 5.1: expressing numbers as 7k + r and reasoning about what r the sum carries). Problem 2 needs the digit-sum and alternating-digit-sum divisibility rules (section 5.2: place-value algebra for 9 and 11). Problem 3 needs the always/sometimes/never divisibility-law framework (section 5.1: if a divides M and a divides N then a divides M ± N, and the LCM law). Problem 4 needs cryptarithm reasoning — units-digit constraint then bounding (section 5.3). Watch for: in Problem 1, students writing the sum of two remainder expressions without reducing the combined remainder mod 7; in Problem 2, students applying the digit-sum rule to check divisibility by 11 instead of the alternating rule; in Problem 3, students confusing 'divisible by both 6 and 10' with 'divisible by 60' without checking that 6 and 10 share the factor 2; in Problem 4, students not using the units-digit of KKK to pin K before trying other digits.

visual_aids.title: Problems and solutions
visual_aids.table:
No. | Problem | Solution
1 | A number N leaves remainder 4 when divided by 7, and a number M leaves remainder 5 when divided by 7. Without dividing, find the remainder when (i) N + M and (ii) N × M are each divided by 7. | Write N = 7a + 4 and M = 7b + 5. (i) N + M = 7(a + b) + 9 = 7(a + b + 1) + 2, so the remainder is 2. (ii) N × M = (7a + 4)(7b + 5) = 49ab + 35a + 28b + 20 = 7(7ab + 5a + 4b + 2) + 6, so the remainder is 6.
2 | A six-digit number has the form 3A5B72, where A and B are single digits. Find all pairs (A, B) such that the number is divisible by both 9 and 11. | Divisibility by 9: digit sum = 3 + A + 5 + B + 7 + 2 = 17 + A + B must be divisible by 9, so A + B = 1 or A + B = 10 (since A, B are digits, A + B ≤ 18; next would be 19, impossible). Divisibility by 11: alternating sum (units upward) = 2 − 7 + B − 5 + A − 3 = A + B − 13 must be 0 or a multiple of 11, so A + B − 13 = 0 giving A + B = 13, or A + B − 13 = −11 giving A + B = 2, or A + B − 13 = 11 giving A + B = 24 (impossible). The two conditions together require A + B to satisfy both lists: {1, 10} ∩ {2, 13} = empty — no pair satisfies both simultaneously. (Teacher note: if the problem is to have a solution, replace 72 with 18: digit sum becomes 3 + A + 5 + B + 1 + 8 = 17 + A + B, same constraint; alternating sum = 8 − 1 + B − 5 + A − 3 = A + B − 1, must be 0 or ±11, giving A + B = 1 or A + B = 12. Intersection with {1, 10}: A + B = 1. With A + B = 1, single-digit pairs: (0,1) and (1,0). Both valid. Use the number 3A5B18 in class.) | Use the number 3A5B18. Digit sum = 3 + A + 5 + B + 1 + 8 = 17 + A + B divisible by 9 → A + B = 1 or A + B = 10. Alternating sum (from units) = 8 − 1 + B − 5 + A − 3 = A + B − 1 must be 0 or ±11 → A + B = 1 or A + B = 12. Intersection: A + B = 1. Digit pairs: (A, B) = (0, 1) giving 305118, and (A, B) = (1, 0) giving 315018. Both are divisible by 9 and by 11.
3 | Riya says: 'If a number is divisible by both 6 and 10, it must be divisible by 60.' Is this always, sometimes, or never true? Give an algebraic justification and a counterexample or proof. | Sometimes true. 6 = 2 × 3 and 10 = 2 × 5 share the factor 2, so LCM(6, 10) = 30, not 60. A number divisible by both 6 and 10 must be divisible by 30. Example: 30 is divisible by 6 (30 = 6 × 5) and by 10 (30 = 10 × 3), but 30 ÷ 60 is not a whole number, so 30 is not divisible by 60. Thus the statement is sometimes true (60 itself works) and sometimes false (30 does not). Algebraic route: write the number as 6a = 10b; the number is a multiple of LCM(6,10) = 30, so it has the form 30k. It equals 60k only when k is even, which need not hold.
4 | Solve the cryptarithm AB × 7 = CBA, where each letter stands for a distinct digit and A ≠ 0. | Units digit: B × 7 ends in A. Tens and hundreds: the product is a three-digit number whose hundreds digit is A and units digit is B, reversing the original tens-and-units. Try values of B whose units digit of 7B equals A, and check that A (the hundreds digit of CBA) matches the leading digit of AB. B = 4: 7 × 4 = 28, so A = 8; AB = 84; 84 × 7 = 588. Hundreds digit is 5, but A = 8 — no. B = 7: repeated digit — ruled out. B = 2: A = 4; AB = 42; 42 × 7 = 294. CBA should have C in hundreds, B = 2 in tens, A = 4 in units: 294 → C = 2, but B = 2 already — digits not distinct. B = 6: 7 × 6 = 42, A = 2; AB = 26; 26 × 7 = 182. CBA: units = 2 = A ✓, tens = 8 = B? B = 6 ≠ 8 — no. B = 8: A = 6 (since 7 × 8 = 56, units digit 6); AB = 68; 68 × 7 = 476. CBA: units = 6 = A ✓, tens = 7 = B? B = 8 ≠ 7 — no. B = 3: A = 1 (7 × 3 = 21); AB = 13; 13 × 7 = 91 — only two digits, not three. B = 5: A = 5 — repeated. B = 9: A = 3 (7 × 9 = 63); AB = 39; 39 × 7 = 273. CBA: units = 3 = A ✓, tens = 7 = B? B = 9 ≠ 7 — no. B = 1: A = 7 (7 × 1 = 7); AB = 71; 71 × 7 = 497. CBA: units = 7 = A ✓, tens = 9 = B? B = 1 ≠ 9 — no. No solution exists for AB × 7 = CBA with all digits distinct. (Use AB × 9 = CBA instead: B = 1, A = 9 — repeated; B = 8, A = 2 (9×8=72): AB = 28, 28×9 = 252 — C=2,B=5,A=2 repeated; B = 9 repeated. Use the cryptarithm MN × 4 = NM: units digit of 4N = M; N=3,M=2: 32×4=128 three digits; N=8,M=2: 4×8=32 units=2=M✓, 28×4=112 three digits; N=2,M=8: 28×4=112 nope. Use AB × 3 = CBA: B×3 units = A; B=5,A=5 repeated; B=7,A=1: AB=17,17×3=51 two digits; B=8,A=4: AB=48,48×3=144,CBA=144,C=1,B=4,A=4 repeated. Use the well-formed cryptarithm MN × 4 = NNM — not standard. Use KL × 9 = MLK: L×9 units=K; L=9 gives K=1(81): KL=19,19×9=171,MLK→M=1=K repeated; L=1,K=9: KL=91 but L=1 means units=9 and 91×9=819,MLK=819,M=8,L=1✓,K=9✓, all distinct. Solution: 91×9=819, so K=9,L=1,M=8.) | Use the cryptarithm KL × 9 = MLK. Units step: L × 9 must end in K. Try L = 1: 9 × 1 = 9, so K = 9. Then KL = 91. Check: 91 × 9 = 819. Write as MLK: M = 8, L = 1, K = 9. All three digits distinct and non-zero. ✓ Solution: K = 9, L = 1, M = 8.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes all four problems on the board, one below the other, and reads each aloud. Students read them over and ask only clarifying questions about what is being asked — no hints yet. Everyone picks up pen and begins.
Individual working time. Every student attempts all four problems in full, writing each step. The teacher circulates silently, noting which problems are stalling most groups, but does not intervene.

Groups of three compare solutions. Any answer that differs is reconstructed step by step from the first line — the group does not move on until the disagreement is resolved by reasoning. Groups that finish early are asked to write one sentence naming the chapter idea each problem used.

One student presents one problem to the class — teacher assigns problems to groups so all four are covered. After each presentation the class, not the presenter, names the chapter method the solution rested on. The teacher writes the method-name on the board beside the problem number.

Teacher reads the four method-names from the board and says: every problem in this chapter gave way the moment you found the right algebraic description of the number — that is the one idea the whole chapter rests on. No further summary.

items.prompt: Which of the following correctly explains why all eight expressions formed by placing '+' or '−' between four consecutive numbers always share the same parity?

options.label: A
options.text: Adding or subtracting consecutive numbers always produces a result divisible by 4.

options.label: B
options.text: Consecutive numbers alternate between odd and even, so their total is always odd.

options.label: C
options.text: Switching one sign from '+' to '−' changes the expression's value by twice the affected number, which is even; so parity cannot change.

options.label: D
options.text: The four numbers cancel each other in pairs, making every expression equal to zero.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option A. Switching any sign from '+' to '−' changes the value by 2 times the affected number — an even change — so the parity of all eight expressions remains identical.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the sign-switching argument: each switch changes the value by 2 × (affected number), preserving parity throughout.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student conflates 'same parity' with 'divisible by 4', not recognising that parity is about divisibility by 2 only.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student believes consecutive numbers cancel to zero, confusing a balanced sum with a zero sum.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student incorrectly extends the alternating odd–even pattern of the numbers themselves to the result, ignoring the interaction of the signs.

inclusivity.support: Let the student try {3, 4, 5, 6} with all eight sign patterns and verify parities before reading the algebraic argument.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write the same argument for five numbers and decide whether parity invariance still holds.

exercise.description: Explore whether every natural number, every even number, and 0 (using negatives) can be written as a sum of consecutive numbers; discuss with class.

items.prompt: Priya says: 'For any four integers a, b, c, d, the expressions a + b + c + d and a + b − c + d must have the same parity because a ± b always has the same parity as a + b.' Is Priya correct? Justify your answer using the parity rule for sums and differences.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, Priya is correct. The parity rule states that a ± b has the same parity regardless of whether the sign is '+' or '−': if a and b are both even or both odd, a ± b is even; if one is even and one is odd, a ± b is odd. Applying this rule repeatedly, a ± b ± c ± d always has the same parity no matter which signs are chosen, so a + b + c + d and a + b − c + d share the same parity.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the parity rule for sums and differences iteratively: a ± b ± c ± d always shares parity regardless of sign choices.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student first verify with two specific numbers (e.g., 3 and 4) that 3 + 4 and 3 − 4 have the same parity, then extend to three and four numbers.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: does the same parity-invariance hold if the four integers are not required to be consecutive? Explain why or why not.

exercise.description: Is there a way to explain why all eight expressions from four numbers share parity? Hint: parity rules for sum/difference of two numbers.

items.prompt: Without evaluating the expression, explain whether 27 × 14 × 35 + 9 × 16 is even or odd. State the parity rule you use at each step.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 27 × 14 × 35: the factor 14 is even, so the entire product is even (a product is even if any factor is even). 9 × 16: the factor 16 is even, so this product is even. Even + even = even. Therefore 27 × 14 × 35 + 9 × 16 is even.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the rule 'a product is even if any factor is even' to each term, then use 'even ± even is even'.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to first identify the parity of each individual factor, then use the multiplication rule before tackling the addition.
inclusivity.challenge: Change 14 to 15 and 16 to 15; ask the student to re-examine parity and explain whether the conclusion changes.

exercise.book_ref: Breaking Even — arithmetic expressions, section 5.1 p.115
exercise.description: Without computing, determine which of the eight arithmetic expressions (43+37; 672−348; 4×347×3; 708−477; 809+214; 119×303; 543−479; 513³) are even.

items.prompt: Statement: 'If 8 divides M and 8 divides N, then 8 divides M + N and 8 divides M − N.' Is this statement always, sometimes, or never true? Write a complete algebraic justification for your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Always true. Since 8 divides M, write M = 8p for some integer p. Since 8 divides N, write N = 8q for some integer q. Then M + N = 8p + 8q = 8(p + q), which is a multiple of 8. Similarly, M − N = 8p − 8q = 8(p − q), which is a multiple of 8. So both M + N and M − N are divisible by 8.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Write M = 8p and N = 8q, then factor 8 from M ± N = 8(p ± q) to show divisibility.

inclusivity.support: Encourage the student to try M = 16, N = 24 first to confirm the claim numerically before writing the algebraic argument.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if 8 divides M + N, does it follow that 8 divides both M and N separately? Give an example or counterexample.

exercise.book_ref: Always, Sometimes, or Never — examine statements, section 5.1 p.118
exercise.description: We know the sum of two multiples of 2 is a multiple of 2. Determine if statement 1 (if 8 divides two numbers separately it divides their sum) is also true with subtraction.

items.prompt: Using the place-value decomposition of a four-digit number, which of the following correctly explains why the remainder when any number is divided by 9 equals its digit sum?

options.label: A
options.text: 9 is one less than 10, so dividing by 9 always gives a remainder equal to the number of digits.

options.label: B
options.text: Each digit contributes its face value multiplied by 9 to the number, so 9 divides out leaving only the digits.

options.label: C
options.text: Each power of 10 leaves remainder 1 when divided by 9, so the remainder of the entire number equals the sum of its digits times 1, which is the digit sum.

options.label: D
options.text: The digit sum rule works because 9 × 1, 9 × 11, 9 × 111, … are all repunits, which divide any number.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option A. Since 10 ≡ 1 (mod 9), 100 ≡ 1 (mod 9), 1000 ≡ 1 (mod 9), and so on, a number written as a·1000 + b·100 + c·10 + d leaves the same remainder as a·1 + b·1 + c·1 + d = a + b + c + d when divided by 9.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use 10^n ≡ 1 (mod 9) for all n ≥ 0 so the number's remainder equals the sum of its digit coefficients.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student confuses the relationship between 9 and 10 with a rule about digit count rather than digit values.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student incorrectly thinks each digit is multiplied by 9 in the place-value expansion, reversing the actual structure.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses the repunit multiples of 9 (999…9) with repunits (111…1) and inverts the argument.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to build the remainder table for 10, 100, 1000 divided by 9 from direct division before reading the algebraic proof.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to construct the analogous argument for divisibility by 3 and verify it gives the same digit-sum rule.

exercise.description: Can any number made of only digits '0' and '9' (in any order) always be divisible by 9?

items.prompt: Explain why the divisibility-by-11 shortcut uses an alternating digit sum (subtracting even-position digits and adding odd-position digits) rather than a simple digit sum. Use the remainder of powers of 10 when divided by 11 in your explanation.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: When any power of 10 is divided by 11, the remainder alternates: 10^0 = 1 gives remainder 1; 10^1 = 10 gives remainder 10 ≡ −1 (mod 11); 10^2 = 100 gives remainder 1; 10^3 gives remainder −1; and so on. So odd-positioned place values contribute +1 times their digit and even-positioned place values contribute −1 times their digit to the remainder. The number is divisible by 11 exactly when this alternating sum is 0 or a multiple of 11.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use 10^n ≡ (−1)^n (mod 11), giving alternating +1/−1 weights to digits at successive positions.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to compute 10 mod 11, 100 mod 11, and 1000 mod 11 by direct division first, then look for the alternating pattern.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if the alternating digit sum equals 11, what is the remainder when the number is divided by 11? Justify algebraically.

exercise.description: Using the alternating place-value pattern, determine whether 462 is divisible by 11.

items.prompt: Which of the following statements about divisibility by 9 and digit sums is always true?

options.label: A
options.text: If a number is divisible by 9, its digit sum is divisible by 9; AND if a number's digit sum is divisible by 9, the number is divisible by 9.

options.label: B
options.text: If a number is divisible by 9, its digit sum is divisible by 9; but a number whose digit sum is divisible by 9 is not necessarily divisible by 9.

options.label: C
options.text: If a number's digit sum is not divisible by 9, the number could still be divisible by 9.

options.label: D
options.text: The digit sum of a number divisible by 9 is always a single digit.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option A. The remainder of a number divided by 9 equals the digit sum's remainder divided by 9 (by the place-value proof), so divisibility by 9 and divisibility of the digit sum by 9 are equivalent — both directions hold.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The place-value proof establishes that number ≡ digit sum (mod 9), making the divisibility relationship a biconditional.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student accepts the forward implication but wrongly doubts the reverse, not realising the proof gives an equivalence (≡), not just a one-way implication.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student believes a counterexample to the digit-sum rule might exist, failing to trust the algebraic proof that the two remainders are always equal.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses 'digit sum divisible by 9' with 'digit sum equals 9', ignoring multiples of 9 with two-digit digit sums such as 99 (digit sum 18).

inclusivity.support: Let the student check 9, 18, 27, 36 and their digit sums to build confidence in both directions before reading the proof.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to state and verify the analogous biconditional for divisibility by 3.

exercise.description: Examine which of four statements about divisibility by 9 and digit sums are correct: (i) divisible by 9 ⟹ digit sum divisible by 9; (ii) digit sum divisible by 9 ⟹ divisible by 9; (iii) not divisible by 9 ⟹ digit sum not divisible by 9; (iv) digit sum not divisible by 9 ⟹ not divisible by 9.

items.prompt: Find the smallest positive integer that leaves a remainder of 4 when divided by 7. Write an algebraic expression that generates all positive integers leaving remainder 4 when divided by 7, and verify that your first two values are correct.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The smallest positive integer leaving remainder 4 when divided by 7 is 4 itself (since 4 = 7×0 + 4). The general expression is 7k + 4 for non-negative integers k. For k = 0: 4 ÷ 7 = 0 remainder 4. For k = 1: 11 ÷ 7 = 1 remainder 4. Both verified.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the remainder representation: any integer leaving remainder r when divided by d has the form dk + r; the smallest positive case is r itself when r > 0.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to list the first ten multiples of 7 and add 4 to each; this builds the pattern before the algebraic form is written.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: write two different algebraic expressions that generate the same set of integers, and verify they are equivalent.

exercise.description: Find a number that has a remainder of 3 when divided by 5; write more such numbers.

items.prompt: A number is divisible by 36. Using divisibility rules, explain why it must also be divisible by 9 and by 4. Then decide: is a number divisible by both 9 and 4 necessarily divisible by 36? Justify your answer with the relevant general law.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 36 = 4 × 9. Since 36 divides the number, all factors of 36 also divide it (the law: if A is divisible by k, it is divisible by all factors of k). So the number is divisible by both 9 and 4. Conversely, since 4 and 9 are coprime (share no common prime factor), a number divisible by both is divisible by their product 4 × 9 = 36. This is the LCM law: if a number is divisible by two coprime integers k and m, it is divisible by k × m = lcm(k, m). Verified: e.g. 36 is divisible by 9 (digit sum 9) and by 4 (last two digits 36 ÷ 4 = 9), and indeed 36 ÷ 36 = 1.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply 'divisible by k implies divisible by all factors of k' for the forward direction; apply the LCM law for coprime k, m for the converse.

inclusivity.support: Let the student check divisibility of 72 and 108 by 9, 4, and 36 using the digit-sum and last-two-digits shortcuts before attempting the general argument.
inclusivity.challenge: Change 9 and 4 to 6 and 4 and ask whether divisibility by both 6 and 4 guarantees divisibility by 24; explain why the answer differs.

exercise.book_ref: Always, Sometimes, or Never — extra statements, section 5.1 p.121
exercise.description: Determine for statements 6–8: (6) if divisible by both 9 and 4, must be divisible by 36; (7) if divisible by both 6 and 4, must be divisible by 24; (8) odd + even gives a multiple of 6 — always, sometimes, or never true.

items.prompt: An 8-digit number has digital root 7. What is the digital root of the number obtained by adding 9 to it? What is the digital root of the number obtained by adding 20 to the original number? Show your reasoning for each.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Adding 9: since 9 is a multiple of 9 and the digital root measures the remainder on division by 9, adding 9 does not change the remainder mod 9. The digital root remains 7. Adding 20: 20 = 18 + 2, so adding 20 increases the remainder mod 9 by 2 (since 18 is a multiple of 9). New remainder = 7 + 2 = 9 ≡ 0 (mod 9). A remainder of 0 corresponds to digital root 9. Verification (forward): pick any number with digital root 7, e.g. 7. 7 + 9 = 16, digital root of 16 = 1 + 6 = 7. Correct. 7 + 20 = 27, digital root of 27 = 9. Correct.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the fact that digital root = remainder mod 9 (with 9 substituted for remainder 0); adding a multiple of 9 does not change the digital root.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to pick a specific number with digital root 7 (e.g., 25) and directly compute the digital roots of 25 + 9 and 25 + 20 before generalising.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: what is the digital root of the original number raised to the power 2? Use the digital-root-mod-9 connection to answer without computing.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.2 p.131
exercise.description: The digital root of an 8-digit number is 5. What is the digital root of 10 more than that number?

items.prompt: In the cryptarithm AB × 6 = CBA, each letter represents a distinct digit and A ≠ 0, C ≠ 0. Find the values of A, B, and C.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: AB is a two-digit number; CBA is a three-digit number. So AB × 6 ≥ 100, giving AB ≥ 17. Also AB × 6 ≤ 999, giving AB ≤ 166 — but AB is two-digit, so AB ≤ 99. The product CBA has its units digit A and hundreds digit C, with the tens digit B matching the tens digit of AB. Units column: the units digit of 6 × B must equal A (since the units digit of CBA is A). Hundreds: C is the hundreds digit of 6 × AB. Try A = 1: units digit of 6B = 1 — impossible (6B ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8 only, never 1). Try A = 2: 6B ends in 2, so B = 2 or B = 7. If B = 2: AB = 22, 22 × 6 = 132, CBA would be 221 — but B in CBA (tens digit of 132 is 3) ≠ 2. If B = 7: AB = 27, 27 × 6 = 162, CBA = 162 means C = 1, B = 6, A = 2 — but B is supposed to be 7, contradiction. Try A = 4: 6B ends in 4, so B = 4 or B = 9. B = 4: AB = 44, 44 × 6 = 264, CBA = 264: C = 2, B = 6, A = 4 — B should be 4, contradiction. B = 9: AB = 49, 49 × 6 = 294, CBA = 294: C = 2, B = 9, A = 4 — matches! A = 4, B = 9, C = 2. Distinct digits: 4, 9, 2. All non-zero. Verified: 49 × 6 = 294.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Bound AB by requiring a three-digit product, use the units-digit constraint on B from 6 × B ≡ A (mod 10), and verify the full product digit-by-digit.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student list all two-digit numbers AB for which 6 × AB is a three-digit number, then check each for the digit-reversal property.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: are there other solutions if we allow A = C? Explain why the constraint that letters represent distinct digits rules them out or admits them.

items.prompt: Three numbers each leave a remainder of 2 when divided by 6. Rashida claims their sum is always a multiple of 6. Verify or refute her claim algebraically, and if true, state which general divisibility law guarantees the result.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Write the three numbers as 6p + 2, 6q + 2, and 6r + 2. Their sum is (6p + 2) + (6q + 2) + (6r + 2) = 6p + 6q + 6r + 6 = 6(p + q + r + 1). This is a multiple of 6, so Rashida's claim is true. The general law used: if a number can be written as 6 times an integer, it is divisible by 6; equivalently, the sum of quantities each leaving remainder 2 on division by 6 has total remainder 3 × 2 = 6 ≡ 0 (mod 6). Verification: e.g. 8, 14, 20 each leave remainder 2 when divided by 6; 8 + 14 + 20 = 42 = 6 × 7. Confirmed.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Write each number as 6k + 2 and sum: three such terms yield 6(p + q + r + 1), directly a multiple of 6.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to try three specific numbers leaving remainder 2 on division by 6 (e.g., 2, 8, 14) and check divisibility of the sum before writing the algebraic argument.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: does the same result hold for four such numbers? What about n such numbers — for which values of n is the sum always a multiple of 6?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 5.1 p.122
exercise.description: Tathagat claims that adding any three numbers that each leave remainder 2 when divided by 6 always gives a multiple of 6. Is this true?
